subtitles.text: What if you could run GPT-2 using nothing but CSS?
No JavaScript, no WebAssembly. Just stylesheets and fonts, running a 124 million parameter transformer.
Here's how Shubham Patil pulled it off.
CSS can already do arithmetic with calc, plus exp, pow, and square root.
But unregistered variables are stored as expressions, which unroll into giant chains. Registering them with at-property forces the browser to store real numbers.
Arithmetic is easy. The hard part is matrix multiplication, and the trick is variable fonts.
In a variable font, each axis shifts a glyph's advance width by a stored delta.
So a glyph's width is its default width, plus the sum of deltas times axis values. That's a dot product.
Set the axes to the input vector, give each glyph one row of weights, and a line of glyphs becomes a matrix-vector multiply.
Chromium caps fonts at 256 axes, so each 768-dimension input is split across three fonts, with weights stored as nine-bit integers.
To read a width back as a number, the glyph drives a scroll-linked view timeline.
In a container of width V, animation progress is V over V plus w. Solve for w, and the width falls right out.
Tokenizing uses ligatures. GPT-2's byte-pair merges become font substitutions, and each token's glyph is its ID plus one units wide.
Embeddings use font regions. Two axes select one of fifty thousand regions, whose deltas hold that token's 768-number vector.
Attention needs q times k, two dynamic values. A region spanning two axes has strength q times k, which gives the product.
Softmax uses max and exp. And the KV cache lives in CSS transitions with a one-day delay, holding past keys and values in place.
The twelve blocks must run in order. Running them all in one pass let errors pile up to an RMS of ten.
So one set of elements is reused. A pass variable selects each block's fonts through container style queries, and an SVG set element advances the pass.
The final layer gives 50,257 logits. Each word gets a box clamped to one pixel if it's the max, and zero otherwise, so only the winner shows.
For sampling, Gumbel noise stored in a font is added to each logit, scaled by temperature. The widest box wins.
It's slow. About fifteen to fifty seconds per token, a quarter gigabyte of fonts, and up to six gigabytes of RAM.
But it matches Python GPT-2 token for token. A full transformer, running inside the browser's rendering engine.
